body: The trachea is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the tubular airway connecting the larynx to the main bronchi. Parameters: (1) the cartilaginous framework — approximately 16-20 C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, open posteriorly and connected by the trachealis muscle; (2) the mucosal lining — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells that propel trapped particles upward via the mucociliary escalator; (3) the length and position — approximately 11 cm long in adults, extending from the larynx at the level of C6 vertebra to the carina at T4-T5 where it bifurcates; (4) the blood supply — supplied by the inferior thyroid arteries and drained by the thyroid venous plexus, innervated by the vagus and sympathetic trunks. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, emergency airway management protocols, and thoracic surgery references. e.g.: the trachea described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; tracheostomy tube placement through the anterior tracheal wall in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; tracheal bifurcation visualized on a PA chest radiograph | not: the bronchus (the tubular airway below the tracheal bifurcation, a distinct structure); the larynx (the structure above the trachea housing the vocal folds, a distinct structure) [formal: trachea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The thyrohyoid membrane is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the broad fibrous sheet extending between the superior border of the thyroid cartilage and the hyoid bone. Parameters: (1) the attachments — inferiorly attached to the superior border and superior horns of the thyroid cartilage, superiorly to the superior margin and tips of the greater horns of the hyoid bone; (2) the composition — a broad fibrous sheet with a thicker anterior margin and thinner posterior portions; (3) the relationships — anteriorly continuous with the infrahyoid musculature, posteriorly opens into a slit-like interval (the thyrohyoid hiatus) through which the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels pass; (4) the lateral thickening — the lateral margins thicken into the thyrohyoid ligament, which provides the primary structural connection between the hyoid and thyroid cartilages; (5) the clinical access — a landmark for the thyrohyoid membrane puncture technique in percutaneous tracheostomy and a surgical approach window in anterior neck dissection. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, head and neck surgical atlases, and airway management guidelines. e.g.: the thyrohyoid membrane described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; the thyrohyoid membrane as a surgical landmark in anterior neck dissection per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; percutaneous tracheostomy via thyrohyoid membrane puncture in the journal of Critical Care Medicine [formal: membrana thyrohyoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The nasopharynx is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the superior division of the pharynx, lying posterior to the nasal cavity and superior to the soft palate, forming the airway conduit between the nasal choanae and the oropharynx. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly the posterior nasal apertures (choanae), inferiorly the superior border of the soft palate, posteriorly the mucosa overlying the body of the sphenoid and the superior constrictor muscle; (2) the lymphoid tissue — the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) on the posterior wall, and the lateral pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenmüller) on each lateral wall; (3) the epithelial lining — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium continuous with the nasal cavity; (4) the clinical relevance — site of adenoid hypertrophy causing nasal obstruction, and the fossa of Rosenmüller as a common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma. It persists as a standard anatomical region in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology, and head-and-neck radiology. e.g.: the nasopharynx shown in the pharynx chapter of Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; nasopharyngoscopy for adenoid evaluation per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; nasopharyngeal carcinoma staging using the pharyngeal recess on MRI per AJCC 8th edition | not: the oropharynx (the middle division of the pharynx behind the oral cavity, inferior to the soft palate); the nasal cavity (the air-filled space anterior to the nasopharynx, separated by the choanae); the pharyngeal tonsil (the lymphoid tissue within the nasopharyngeal wall, a structure contained within the space) [formal: nasopharynx | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The corniculate cartilages (cartilagines corniculatae) are a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired conical cartilages that sit atop the apices of the arytenoid cartilages within the larynx, forming part of the posterior laryngeal inlet and supporting the aryepiglottic folds. Parameters: (1) the position — each cartilage rests on the apex of its corresponding arytenoid cartilage; (2) the composition — elastic cartilage, continuous with the arytenoid's cartilage; (3) the relationships — embedded within the aryepiglottic fold, adjacent to the cuneiform cartilage, and contributing to the closure of the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology references, and airway management guides. e.g.: the corniculate cartilage shown in the larynx chapter of Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the corniculate tubercle identified during direct laryngoscopy per Miller's Anesthesia, 9th edition; corniculate cartilage calcification noted on lateral neck radiograph in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the cuneiform cartilage (paired wedge-shaped cartilage in the aryepiglottic fold, anterior to the corniculate); the arytenoid cartilage (larger pyramid-shaped cartilage the corniculate rests upon, a distinct structure); the epiglottis (leaf-shaped cartilage forming the anterior roof of the laryngeal inlet, a distinct structure) [formal: cartilago corniculata | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The superior laryngeal nerve is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the branch of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) that divides into internal and external divisions to supply the larynx above the level of the vocal folds. Parameters: (1) the origin — arises from the inferior vagal ganglion as the vagus nerve passes the inferior ganglion of the inferior salivary nucleus in the jugular foramen; (2) the internal branch — pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to become the internal laryngeal nerve, providing sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds; (3) the external branch — descends on the inferior pharyngeal constrictor to supply the cricothyroid muscle and the superior laryngeal muscles; (4) the anatomical course — travels with the superior laryngeal artery along the thyrohyoid membrane. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology references, and regional anesthesia protocols. e.g.: the superior laryngeal nerve described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; superior laryngeal nerve block for laryngeal surgery in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve tested during sensory evaluation of the larynx | not: the recurrent laryngeal nerve (the other laryngeal branch supplying the larynx below the vocal folds); the vagus nerve (the parent nerve from which the superior laryngeal nerve branches, a distinct structure) [formal: nervus laryngeus superior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The cuneiform cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired nodular elastic cartilages embedded within the substance of the aryepiglottic folds, situated between the corniculate cartilages posteriorly and the lateral margins of the epiglottis anteriorly. Parameters: (1) the position — embedded within the aryepiglottic fold mucosa, lateral to the corniculate cartilage and superior to the arytenoid apex; (2) the composition — elastic cartilage core surrounded by mucous glands and fibroelastic connective tissue; (3) the variability — absent in approximately 25% of individuals (WSN cuneiformis), making its presence a positive anatomical finding on endoscopy; (4) the functional role — stiffens the aryepiglottic fold and contributes to the sphincteric closure of the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It persists as a standard anatomical variant in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and head and neck radiology. e.g.: the cuneiform cartilage described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; cuneiform cartilage visible as a nodule on direct laryngoscopy; identification of the cuneiform cartilage on axial CT imaging | not: the corniculate cartilage (sitting atop the arytenoid apex, not embedded in fold mucosa); the aryepiglottic fold (the mucosal fold that contains the cuneiform cartilage, a distinct structure) [formal: cartilago cuneiformis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The vocal ligament is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the free superior margin of the cricothyroid membrane, forming the elastic fiber core of the vocal fold. Parameters: (1) the attachments — anteriorly anchored to the thyroid cartilage at the angle just behind the laryngeal prominence, posteriorly attached to the vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage; (2) the microstructure — densely packed elastic fibers oriented in the anterior-posterior direction, with collagen fibers providing tensile strength; (3) the mucosal covering — the vocal ligament is covered by respiratory epithelium forming the mucosal layer of the vocal fold; (4) the vibratory mechanism — the ligament provides the stiff elastic scaffold upon which the mucosal wave oscillates during phonation. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and voice research protocols. e.g.: the vocal ligament described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; vocal ligament resection in type I thyroplasty for glottic insufficiency; the vocal ligament as the stiff core of the vocal fold in Hirano's structural model of phonation | not: the vocal fold (the entire structure containing the ligament, not just its core); the cricothyroid membrane (the fibrous sheet from which the ligament derives, a distinct structure) [formal: ligamentum vocale | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The oropharynx is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the middle division of the pharynx, lying posterior to the oral cavity and between the soft palate and the epiglottis, forming the common pathway for both respiratory and digestive streams. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly the oral cavity at the fauces (the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches), superiorly the soft palate and posterior nasal cavities, posteriorly the mucosa overlying the middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles, and inferiorly the level of the hyoid bone and epiglottis; (2) the lymphoid structures — the palatine tonsils between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches, and the lingual tonsil on the posterior third of the tongue; (3) the muscular walls — three constrictor muscles (superior, middle, inferior) and longitudinal muscles (stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus); (4) the clinical relevance — site of tonsillectomy, oropharyngeal dysphagia assessment, and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma. It persists as a standard anatomical region in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology, and head-and-neck surgical atlases. e.g.: the oropharynx shown in the pharynx chapter of Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; oropharyngeal airway placement visualizing the tonsillar fossae per Miller's Anesthesia, 9th edition; oropharyngeal carcinoma assessed by tonsillar pillar inspection in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th ed | not: the nasopharynx (the superior division behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate); the hypopharynx (the inferior division behind the larynx, from the epiglottis to the cricoid); the oral cavity (the space anterior to the oropharynx, separated by the fauces) [formal: oropharynx | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The hyoid bone is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the U-shaped bone in the anterior neck at the level of C3, serving as a floating anchor between the mandible and the larynx. Parameters: (1) the architecture — composed of a body, greater horns (cornua), and lesser horns (cornua), with the greater horns extending posterolaterally from the body; (2) the suspensory attachments — suspended from the styloid processes of the temporal bones by the stylohyoid ligaments and from the mandible by the mylohyoid muscle; (3) the muscular attachments — anteriorly by the suprahyoid muscles (mylohyoid, geniohyoid, digastric, stylohyoid), inferiorly by the infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid); (4) the relationships — lies superior to the thyroid cartilage and laryngeal inlet, anterior to the pharyngeal wall, and connected to the epiglottis by the thyrohyoid membrane; (5) the clinical relevance — a critical landmark in anterior neck surgery, used as a reference for thyroid and parathyroid surgery, and a common site of fracture in strangulation and manual choking. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, head and neck surgical atlases, and forensic medicine references. e.g.: the hyoid bone described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake, Hauser and Carucci; the hyoid bone as a surgical landmark in thyroidectomy per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; forensic analysis of hyoid bone fracture in strangulation cases per the American Journal of Forensic Medicine [formal: os hyoideum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The conus elasticus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the conical sheet of elastic connective tissue extending between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, forming the walls of the subglottic region. Parameters: (1) the origin — arises from the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage, attaching to its entire superior margin; (2) the attachments — ascends anteriorly to the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage, laterally to the vocal ligaments and vocal processes of the arytenoid cartilages, and posteriorly to the interarytenoid muscles; (3) the composition — predominantly elastic fibers with some collagen, thicker inferiorly and tapering as it ascends; (4) the relationships — continuous superiorly with the cricothyroid membrane and with the vocal ligaments (which form its free upper borders), continuous inferiorly with the subglottic mucosa; (5) the clinical relevance — defines the boundaries of the subglottis, a common site for subglottic stenosis, and serves as a surgical landmark during laryngeal procedures. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and head and neck surgical planning documents. e.g.: the conus elasticus described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake, Hauser and Carucci; the conus elasticus as the structural basis of the vocal ligament in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; surgical resection of conus elasticus in laryngeal trauma reconstruction per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition [formal: conus elasticus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The cricothyroid membrane is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the fibrous sheet between the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage and the complete superior border of the cricoid cartilage, forming the floor of the laryngeal cavity and the landmark of the emergency surgical airway. Parameters: (1) the boundaries - superiorly the inferior border of the thyroid laminae, inferiorly the superior border of the cricoid lamina, laterally blending into the cricothyroid joint capsules; (2) the composition - a fibroelastic sheet, thin and transparent anteriorly, with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal vessels passing on its deep surface; (3) the relationships - its free superior border thickens into the vocal ligament, and the submucosa above it carries the laryngeal mucosa; (4) the clinical access - the site of needle cricothyroidotomy and percutaneous dilational cricothyroidotomy, the standard emergency airway when intubation fails. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, emergency airway protocols, and laryngeal surgical planning documents. e.g.: cricothyroid membrane puncture for needle cricothyroidotomy per ATLS 10th edition; the membrane shown in the larynx chapter of Moore Clinically Orientated Anatomy 9th edition; the membrane as the entry point of percutaneous cricothyroidotomy in the ASA difficult airway algorithm | not: the cricoid cartilage (the complete ring forming its inferior border, a distinct structure); the thyrohyoid membrane (the membrane above it between thyroid and hyoid); the cricothyroid joint (the articulation between the cartilages, lateral to the membrane) [formal: membrana cricothyroidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The pharynx is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the muscular tube that connects the posterior nasal apertures and oral cavity to the larynx and esophagus, serving both the respiratory and digestive pathways. Parameters: (1) the superior-to-inferior divisions — nasopharynx (behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate), oropharynx (behind the oral cavity, between the soft palate and epiglottis), and laryngopharynx/hypopharynx (behind the larynx, from the epiglottis to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage where it continues as the esophagus); (2) the muscular walls — three constrictor muscles (superior, middle, inferior) arranged in overlapping tiers plus longitudinal muscles (stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus) that elevate the pharynx and larynx during swallowing; (3) the compartments — the aerodigestive conduit that separates respiratory from digestive flow via the soft palate, epiglottis, and pharyngeal constrictor coordination; (4) the clinical landmarks — Waldeyer ring of lymphoid tissue (adenoids, palatine tonsils, lingual tonsil), the pharyngeal recess of Fossa of Rosenmüller, the esophageal opening. It persists as a maintained anatomical region in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology, and head-and-neck surgical atlases. e.g.: the pharynx as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; nasopharyngeal carcinoma staging per the AJCC 8th edition using the pharyngeal recess; pharyngeal manometry measuring superior, middle, and inferior constrictor pressures | not: the esophagus (the digestive tube continuing from the pharynx at the cricoid level, distinct pathway); the trachea (the respiratory tube continuing from the larynx at the carina, distinct pathway); the oral cavity (the space anterior to the oropharynx, separated by the fauces) [formal: pharynx | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The laryngeal vestibule is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the supraglottic chamber of the larynx between the laryngeal inlet above and the rima glottidis below. Parameters: (1) the boundaries - above the laryngeal inlet (epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoid cartilages), below the free edges of the true vocal folds, laterally opening to the piriform recesses which continue into the pharynx and lie outside this boundary; (2) the contents - the pre-epiglottic space anterior to the epiglottis and the laryngeal ventricle between the vestibular and vocal folds lie within it; (3) the clinical significance - the supraglottic compartment that closes during swallowing as the vestibular folds approximate over it, and the region of supraglottic obstruction treated by supraglottic stenting. It persists as a standard anatomical region in head-and-neck surgical atlases, laryngology texts, and airway management references. e.g.: the laryngeal vestibule delineated in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; the laryngeal vestibule as the supraglottic chamber described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; the laryngeal vestibule shown in the larynx chapter of Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the laryngeal ventricle (the recess between the vestibular and vocal folds within it, a distinct space); the piriform recess (the pharyngeal recess beside the inlet, outside the boundary); the supraglottis (a clinical level of the larynx, overlapping but a distinct classification boundary) [formal: vestibulum laryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The hypopharynx (also called the laryngopharynx) is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the inferior division of the pharynx that lies posterior to the larynx, extending from the epiglottis superiorly to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage inferiorly where it continues as the esophagus. Parameters: (1) the four subsites — postcricoid region (posterior to the cricoid cartilage, anterior to the esophagus), bilateral pyriform sinuses (lateral recesses lateral to the laryngeal inlet, bounded medially by the aryepiglottic fold and laterally by the thyroid cartilage), the posterior pharyngeal wall behind the larynx, and the laryngeal inlet (the opening from the oropharynx into the laryngopharynx bounded by the epiglottis and arytenoids); (2) the mucosal lining — stratified squamous epithelium continuous with both esophageal and laryngeal mucosa; (3) the muscular layer — continuous with the pharyngeal constrictors longitudinally and the superior esophageal sphincter inferiorly; (4) the neurovascular supply — internal laryngeal nerve (sensory, from superior laryngeal branch of vagus), recurrent laryngeal nerve, and superior laryngeal vessels; (5) the clinical significance — common site of squamous cell carcinoma, region assessed during swallowing evaluation, landmark for esophageal opening. It persists as a maintained anatomical region in head-and-neck anatomy, oncology staging systems, and otolaryngology. e.g.: the hypopharynx subsites mapped in TNM staging (AJCC 8th edition) for hypopharyngeal carcinoma; a barium swallow study demonstrating a pyriform sinus filling defect; postcricoid web identified on upper endoscopy | not: the pyriform-fossa (the lateral recess specifically, a subsite of the hypopharynx); the esophagus (the tube continuing from the hypopharynx at the cricoid level, distinct pathway); the larynx (the organ anterior to the hypopharynx containing the vocal folds, distinct functional system) [formal: hypopharynx | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The arytenoid cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired pyramidal cartilages forming the posterior anchor of the vocal fold apparatus within the laryngeal framework. Parameters: (1) the shape — a pyramidal cartilage with a base articulating with the cricoid lamina and an apex directed superiorly; (2) the vocal process — an anterior projection serving as the posterior attachment of the vocal fold; (3) the muscular process — a lateral projection serving as the insertion point for intrinsic laryngeal muscles; (4) the articular facet — a smooth surface articulating with the cricoid cartilage to enable rotation and sliding of the arytenoids. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and airway management guidelines. e.g.: the arytenoid cartilage described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; arytenoid cartilage displacement visible on lateral neck radiograph; arytenoid cartilage repositioning surgery for unilateral vocal fold paralysis in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the corniculate cartilage (a smaller cartilage sitting atop the arytenoid apex); the cricoarytenoid joint (the articulation between the arytenoid and cricoid cartilages, a distinct structure) [formal: cartilago arytenoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The vallecula (epiglottic vallecula) is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired shallow depressions between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis, bounded medially by the median glossoepiglottic fold and laterally opening into the piriform sinuses. Parameters: (1) the anatomical boundaries — anteriorly the posterior surface of the epiglottis, posteriorly the base of the tongue (posterior third, above the circumvallate papillae), bounded medially by the median glossoepiglottic fold and laterally by the lateral glossoepiglottic folds; (2) the bilateral nature — a left and right vallecular space separated by the median fold; (3) the clinical significance — blind spot on routine laryngoscopy that requires epiglottic elevation to visualize, common site for vallecular cysts that can cause airway obstruction, landmark for determining laryngoscopic view (Mallampati classification uses vallecular space to grade airway difficulty), injection site for topical local anesthesia in awake intubation; (4) the developmental anatomy — vallecular cysts arise from obstruction of minor salivary glands in the vallecular mucosa. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in airway management guidelines, otolaryngology texts, and anesthesia reference atlases. e.g.: the valleculae visualized during direct laryngoscopy using a Macintosh blade in Miller's Anesthesia 9th edition; a vallecular cyst causing obstructive sleep apnea imaged on MRI per the Laryngoscope; Mallampati class determination by visualizing the vallecular space in the ASA difficult airway algorithm | not: the piriform-fossa (the lateral recess lateral to the laryngeal inlet, separated by the aryepiglottic fold); the circumvallate-papillae (the row of taste buds anterior to the vallecula on the tongue base, distinct structure) [formal: vallecula | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The laryngeal ventricle is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the hourglass-shaped recess between the superior (vestibular) folds and inferior (vocal) folds within the laryngeal cavity. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly and posteriorly it extends as the laryngeal saccule, a blind pouch that can become distended; medially bounded by the vocal folds inferiorly and vestibular folds superiorly; (2) the mucosal lining — stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the mucosa of both the ventricular and vocal folds; (3) the laryngeal saccule — a vertical pouch extending superiorly from the anterior portion of the ventricle, containing mucous glands and occasionally distended in laryngoceles; (4) the functional significance — the ventricle serves as a space for the free vibration of the vocal fold mucosa, unencumbered by the overlying vestibular fold. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and airway management references. e.g.: the laryngeal ventricle described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; laryngocele arising from distension of the laryngeal saccule in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; visualization of the laryngeal ventricle during indirect laryngoscopy | not: the laryngeal vestibule (the chamber above the vocal folds from the inlet to the folds, a distinct space); the vocal fold (the mucosal structure forming the inferior boundary of the ventricle, a distinct structure) [formal: ventriculus laryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The laryngeal inlet is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the opening connecting the oropharynx to the laryngeal vestibule. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly bounded by the epiglottis, laterally by the aryepiglottic folds, and posteriorly by the arytenoid cartilages; (2) the spatial orientation — angled approximately 45 degrees downward in the upright position, directing the food bolus around the epiglottis and into the esophagus; (3) the protective mechanism — the epiglottis tilts posteriorly and the aryepiglottic folds contract inward during swallowing to close the inlet and protect the airway; (4) the clinical access — the laryngeal inlet is the target of direct and video laryngoscopy for endotracheal intubation, visualized as the dark opening between the epiglottis and the arytenoid cartilages. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, emergency airway management protocols, and laryngology references. e.g.: the laryngeal inlet described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; laryngeal inlet visualization during direct laryngoscopy in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the laryngeal inlet as the target of rapid sequence intubation in emergency medicine | not: the glottis (the region below the laryngeal inlet containing the vocal folds); the laryngeal vestibule (the chamber within the larynx above the vocal folds, a distinct space) [formal: aditus laryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The rima glottidis is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the slit-like opening between the vocal folds and their processes within the glottis. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly bounded by the space between the vocal processes of the arytenoid cartilages, posteriorly by the space between the body of the arytenoid cartilages; (2) the functional states — widened to the triangle of the respiratory rima during breathing (abducted vocal folds), narrowed to the slit of phonation during voiced speech (adducted vocal folds), and fully closed during coughing and Valsalva; (3) the measurement — approximately 10 mm in length and 3-4 mm in width during quiet breathing in adults; (4) the clinical significance — the narrowest dimension of the rima glottidis determines the airflow resistance during phonation and the minimum endotracheal tube size that can pass through an adducted airway. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology, and airway management guidelines. e.g.: the rima glottidis described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; measurement of the rima glottidis during laryngeal electromyography; the rima glottidis evaluated by stroboscopy in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the glottis (the entire anatomical region including the vocal folds and rima, not just the opening); the laryngeal inlet (the opening to the larynx above the vocal folds, a distinct structure) [formal: rima glottidis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
